title: Paint with radar
blurb: Radar has no colours. Scientists put three radar layers into red, green and blue to see forest, clearings and rivers at a glance. Make your own radar painting of the Amazon!
why: Each radar layer shows something different: HH bounces off the ground, HV is twisted by leaves, and HH÷HV is big where leaves are gone. Mixed as red, green and blue, they paint the forest green and the clearings purple.

title: Flood detector
blurb: Every radar picture is a bit grainy, so everything changes a little between two dates. How much darker must a place get before we call it flooded? Tune the detector like NISAR's scientists did for the Limpopo flood.
why: Choosing the threshold is a real science decision: too low and radar noise looks like flood, too high and real water is missed.

title: Speckle cleaner
blurb: Radar echoes from many tiny things mix, so every pixel flickers: that's called speckle. Clean the Mississippi Delta picture so the water and the marsh are clear, without blurring the shore.
why: Averaging neighbouring pixels (scientists call it multi-looking) removes speckle, but too much makes the edges fuzzy. The best picture is in between.

title: Echo sorter
blurb: Different places send back different echoes. Listen to four places in the Jezreel Valley and sort them from the weakest echo to the strongest.
why: Smooth surfaces send the wave away (weak echo), rough ones scatter some back, and buildings act like corner mirrors (strongest echo).
